prompt: The shop's Ingress is applied to a cluster with no ingress controller in it. What happens?
hint: Look at what `kubectl get ingress` printed in the lab.

choices.text: The API server refuses it, because the cluster has no IngressClass to match
choices.why: It was created: the API server stores an Ingress whether or not anything will read it.

choices.text: It is stored and nothing routes by it; its address stays empty
choices.why: Right. An address is written back by a controller, and with none the Ingress is a record nobody reads.

choices.text: kube-proxy serves it on port 80 of every node
choices.why: kube-proxy implements Services, not Ingress objects; it never reads one.

choices.text: The Service it names gets an external load balancer instead
choices.why: Only a Service of type LoadBalancer asks for one, and the Ingress changes nothing about the Service.

prompt: The shop's Ingress was written for AGIC. Why would moving to ingress-nginx mean rewriting it, though both read the same resource?
hint: Which part of the file is Kubernetes's, and which part is a controller's?

choices.text: ingress-nginx reads a different apiVersion of the Ingress
choices.why: Both read `networking.k8s.io/v1`; the resource is the same.

choices.text: Its probe path and draining are annotations, and only AGIC reads `appgw.ingress.kubernetes.io/`
choices.why: Right. What the fields cannot say goes into annotations, and each controller has its own prefix and spelling.

choices.text: An Ingress is bound to its controller when it is created and cannot move
choices.why: Nothing binds it; a class name or annotation only says which controller should read it.

choices.text: ingress-nginx needs one Ingress per Service
choices.why: One Ingress may name several Services across its rules; the canary is where nginx asks for a second Ingress.

prompt: Which of these can the Ingress resource express in its own fields, with no annotation? Choose all that apply.
hint: Host, path, backend, certificate, class: that is the vocabulary.

choices.text: Requests for shop.example.com go to the shop
choices.why: A rule matches a host.

choices.text: Ten per cent of requests go to the shop at 1.1
choices.why: There is no weight field; ingress-nginx does it with a second, annotated Ingress.

choices.text: Paths under /orders go to the Service shop-v1-0
choices.why: A path with pathType Prefix naming a backend Service and port.

choices.text: Requests carrying the header x-shop-canary go elsewhere
choices.why: A header match is not in the Ingress API; it is an annotation or an HTTPRoute.

choices.text: TLS for the host, with the certificate in a Secret
choices.why: The `tls` entry names the Secret.

prompt: The Kubernetes documentation recommends Gateway instead of Ingress and says the Ingress API has been ___: it stays available and supported, and is no longer developed.
hint: One word for an API that will not change again.

prompt: A cluster uses the application routing add-on's managed NGINX. According to Microsoft's documentation read on 30 October 2026, what should its team plan?
hint: Upstream Ingress NGINX was retired.

choices.text: Nothing: the add-on replaces NGINX in place, and the Ingress objects keep working
choices.why: The successor reads the Gateway API, so the Ingress objects have to be rewritten as routes.

choices.text: Moving to AGIC, which Microsoft now recommends for new clusters
choices.why: AGIC's own pages point at Application Gateway for Containers instead.

choices.text: A move to the add-on's Gateway API implementation or to Application Gateway for Containers before support ends in November 2026
choices.why: Right. Microsoft patches critical security issues in the add-on's NGINX until then, and names those two destinations.

choices.text: Pinning the add-on's NGINX version so that it is never upgraded
choices.why: An unpatched proxy at the front door is the risk the retirement notice is about.

prompt: With AGIC, where does a request to the shop pass through the AGIC pod?
hint: AGIC writes configuration; something else carries requests.

choices.text: At every request, because AGIC is the proxy in front of the pods
choices.why: That is NGINX's arrangement. AGIC carries no requests.

choices.text: Only on the first request to a new pod, to register it
choices.why: A new pod reaches the gateway through a configuration write, never through a request.

choices.text: Nowhere: the gateway sends requests straight to pod addresses
choices.why: Right. AGIC watches the cluster and rewrites the gateway through ARM; the traffic never touches it.

choices.text: On requests that fail the gateway's health probe
choices.why: The probe is the gateway's, built from the pod's readiness probe; AGIC does not handle requests.

prompt: A pod of the shop is replaced during a rolling update. Put in order what happens before the Application Gateway sends requests to the new pod.
hint: The change starts in the cluster and ends outside it.
items: The new pod becomes ready and its address enters the Service's endpoints
AGIC sees the change through the API server
AGIC computes the gateway's new configuration
AGIC sends the configuration to Azure Resource Manager
The Application Gateway applies it and adds the address to its backend pool
trap: Until the last step the gateway still has the old address, which is why connection draining exists.

prompt: The shop answers `/` with a 404. Its Deployment has no readiness probe and its Ingress no `health-probe-path`. What does AGIC's gateway do?
hint: What does AGIC probe when nothing tells it otherwise, and which statuses count as healthy?

choices.text: It probes /healthz, which every container image is expected to have
choices.why: Nothing tells AGIC about /healthz unless a probe or the annotation names it.

choices.text: It skips health checks for pods without a readiness probe
choices.why: The gateway always probes; without a pod probe, AGIC fills in defaults.

choices.text: It sends requests anyway, since the pods are Ready in Kubernetes
choices.why: Readiness in Kubernetes and health at the gateway are two separate verdicts.

choices.text: It probes `/`, gets 404 outside 200 to 399, and marks every pod unhealthy
choices.why: Right. With no probe AGIC uses the Ingress path, and a 404 is not a healthy answer, so the gateway serves nothing.

prompt: An Application Gateway already serves another site through a listener created by hand. AGIC is then pointed at it with default settings. What happens to that listener?
hint: Who does AGIC think the gateway belongs to?

choices.text: AGIC removes it within seconds, because by default it owns the whole gateway
choices.why: Right. AGIC overwrites any configuration no Ingress describes; shared mode, Helm only, is the way around it.

choices.text: AGIC leaves it alone, because it only touches what it created
choices.why: That is shared mode, which is not the default and needs the Helm installation.

choices.text: AGIC refuses to start until the listener is removed
choices.why: It does not refuse; it takes the gateway over.

choices.text: The listener is copied into a new Ingress in the default namespace
choices.why: AGIC writes from the cluster to the gateway, never the other way round.

prompt: Match each AGIC setting to what it does.
hint: Two are flags of the add-on, two are annotations on the Ingress.

pairs.right: Creates a gateway in a new subnet of that size
Uses an Application Gateway that already exists
Reduces 502s while pods are being removed
Sets the path the gateway probes

right_distractors: Sends a share of the traffic to a canary

prompt: Match each Gateway API resource to the owner the API was designed around.
hint: One file per owner; the grant is written by the side being referred to.

pairs.right: The team that runs the cluster
The team that ships the application
The owners of the namespace referred to

right_distractors: The API server, on its own

prompt: A rule of an HTTPRoute lists two backends with weights 3 and 1. What percentage of the rule's requests goes to the second backend?
hint: A weight is divided by the sum of the weights in its list.

prompt: A request for shop.example.com carries `x-shop-canary: yes`. Both rules of the shop's route match `/`. Which rule does a conforming controller apply?
hint: Exact path, longest prefix, method, then...

choices.text: `everyone`, because a weighted rule outranks a single backend
choices.why: Weights play no part in choosing a rule; they only split the chosen rule's requests.

choices.text: `testers`, because with equal paths the match with more header matches wins
choices.why: Right. Both have a PathPrefix of `/` and no method, and `testers` has one header against none.

choices.text: Whichever the controller chooses, as the order is implementation-specific
choices.why: The specification fixes the order for path, method, header and query matches.

choices.text: Both, so the request is sent to 1.0 and to 1.1
choices.why: One request goes to one backend of one rule.

prompt: Which mistakes in an HTTPRoute does `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` refuse, with no controller installed? Choose all that apply.
hint: The definition carries its own validation; existence is a controller's question.

choices.text: A PathPrefix whose value is `orders`
choices.why: The definition requires an absolute path starting with `/`.

choices.text: A backend Service named without a port
choices.why: A rule in the definition: a Service reference must have a port.

choices.text: A backend Service that does not exist
choices.why: Accepted: the API server does not look. A controller would report it, and answer its share with 500.

choices.text: Weights of 90 and 30, which add up to 120
choices.why: Accepted, and correct: weights are proportions, and their sum does not have to be 100.

choices.text: A weight of 1000001
choices.why: The definition sets a maximum of 1,000,000.

prompt: The shop's route sends 90 to `shop-v1-0` and 10 to `shop-v1-1`. A typo renames the first backend to `shop-v1-2`, which does not exist, and the API server accepts it. Under a conforming controller, what percentage of that rule's requests is answered with a 500?
hint: An invalid backend's share of the requests gets 500s.

prompt: On the bring-your-own strategy, the cluster team deletes the shop's Gateway. What happens to its Application Gateway for Containers frontend?
hint: Who created the frontend, and where?

choices.text: The ALB Controller deletes it along with the Gateway
choices.why: That is the managed strategy, where the controller created the frontend.

choices.text: It stays in Azure with its FQDN, because the Azure administrator owns it
choices.why: Right. On bring-your-own you created it in Azure, and only you delete it.

choices.text: It is moved to the next Gateway created in the cluster
choices.why: A frontend is referenced by name from a Gateway; nothing moves it on its own.

choices.text: Azure keeps it for a grace period and then deletes it
choices.why: The documentation describes no grace period; the frontend is the administrator's to delete.

prompt: Three Application Gateway for Containers resources, each with one association, will share one delegated subnet. By Microsoft's rule, how many addresses must that subnet have available?
hint: Each association assumes at least 256.

prompt: Four slips were made in `agc.bicep`: a chosen `fqdn` on the frontend, `subnet` for `subnets`, a `/26`, and a misspelt delegation. What did `bicep build` say?
hint: The compiler checks the type, not the documentation.

choices.text: One warning per slip, four in all
choices.why: Three of them are strings the type does not restrict, and they passed in silence.

choices.text: Nothing at all: it only checks syntax
choices.why: It checks properties against the resource type, which is how it caught the read-only one.

choices.text: A refusal of the `/26`, smaller than the documented `/24`
choices.why: An address prefix is a string to the compiler; the `/24` rule lives in the documentation.

choices.text: One warning, BCP073: `fqdn` is read-only
choices.why: Right. The FQDN is Azure's to generate, and the type says so; the other three compiled cleanly.

prompt: In Application Gateway for Containers, the child resource that is one entry point for clients, with a name Azure generates, is a ___.
hint: A CNAME can point at it.

prompt: The ALB Controller's managed identity is given Contributor on the Application Gateway for Containers resource. Why is that not enough?
hint: Control actions and data actions are different permissions.

choices.text: Contributor cannot be given to a managed identity
choices.why: Any role can be assigned to a managed identity; the question is what the role allows.

choices.text: The controller signs in with a client secret, not the identity
choices.why: It uses the identity through workload identity, the federated credential of lesson 13.

choices.text: Its built-in role has data actions that Owner and Contributor lack
choices.why: Right. AppGw for Containers Configuration Manager carries them, so it is the role to assign.

choices.text: Contributor is too broad, and Azure refuses roles wider than needed
choices.why: Azure assigns broad roles without complaint; the problem is a missing permission, not an excess.

prompt: The shop wants a 90/10 canary written as an HTTPRoute, and a proxy that Azure operates outside the cluster. Which option of this lesson fits?
hint: Two requirements: what it reads, and where the proxy runs.

choices.text: AGIC as an add-on
choices.why: The proxy is outside, but AGIC reads only Ingress and has no weighted split.

choices.text: The application routing add-on's Gateway API implementation
choices.why: It reads routes, but its gateways are pods on the cluster's own nodes.

choices.text: Application Gateway for Containers
choices.why: Right. It reads the Gateway API and its data plane is Azure-operated, outside the cluster.

choices.text: The add-on's managed NGINX, with canary annotations
choices.why: It runs in the cluster, reads Ingress, and its support ends in November 2026.

prompt: A Gateway's conditions read `Accepted=Unknown Pending: Waiting for controller`. What wrote that?
hint: Was a controller ever there?

choices.text: The controller, to say it is still provisioning the gateway
choices.why: A controller that had seen it would write `True` or `False` with its own reason.

choices.text: The definition's default for status, so an unclaimed gateway says so
choices.why: Right. Nothing has claimed the class, and the default is all there is.

choices.text: The API server, after failing to reach the gateway's address
choices.why: The API server never contacts a gateway; it has no address to try.

choices.text: kubectl, while waiting for the apply to finish
choices.why: The conditions are stored in the object; kubectl only printed them.

prompt: Which of these are true of both AGIC and Application Gateway for Containers? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare where the proxy runs, what runs in the cluster, and what each reads.

choices.text: The proxy that carries requests runs outside the cluster
choices.why: An Application Gateway for one, an Azure-operated data plane for the other.

choices.text: A controller pod in the cluster turns Kubernetes resources into Azure configuration
choices.why: AGIC for one, the ALB Controller for the other.

choices.text: They read Gateway API routes
choices.why: Only Application Gateway for Containers does; AGIC reads Ingress alone.

choices.text: They read Ingress objects
choices.why: AGIC reads nothing else, and Application Gateway for Containers reads both.

choices.text: By default they take over an existing gateway and its listeners
choices.why: That is AGIC's ownership of an Application Gateway; Application Gateway for Containers has frontends of its own.

prompt: The shop's HTTPRoute in the namespace `shop` attached to `shop-gateway` in `infra` with no ReferenceGrant. Why was none needed?
hint: One cross-namespace reference is controlled from the gateway's side.

choices.text: ReferenceGrant is only needed for Services in another cluster
choices.why: It covers references across namespaces within a cluster.

choices.text: Routes may refer to anything in any namespace
choices.why: A route naming a Service in `finance` needs the finance team's grant.

choices.text: The grant is created automatically when the route is applied
choices.why: Nothing creates one; it is written by the owners of the namespace referred to.

choices.text: Attachment to a gateway is the exception: its `allowedRoutes` selected the namespace
choices.why: Right. The gateway accepts routes from namespaces labelled `gateway-access: "true"`, and `shop` is one.
